title: De Bello Hispaniensi
author: Pseudo-Caesar
source: Translated by Claude from phi0430.phi001.perseus-lat1, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: Insequenti tempore Caesar castris castra contulit et bracchium ad flumen Salsum ducere coepit. Hic dum in opere nostri distenti essent, complures ex superiore loco adversariorum decucurrerunt nec desinentibus nostris multis telis iniectis compluris vulneribus adfecere. Hic tum, ut ait Ennius, nostri cessere parumper. Itaque praeter consuetudinem eum a nostris animadversum esset cedere, centuriones ex legione V. flumen transgressi duo restituerunt aciem, acriterque eximia virtute pluris eum agerent, ex superiore loco multitudine telorum alter corum concidit.
passages.english: In the period that followed, Caesar moved his camp up close to [the enemy's] camp and began to carry a connecting wall down to the river Salsum. Here, while our men were spread out on the work, a number of the enemy ran down from the higher ground, and, since our men did not let up, they hurled many missiles and wounded a good number of them. Here then, as Ennius says, our men gave way for a little while. And so, when it was noticed that our men were giving way contrary to their custom, two centurions from the Fifth Legion crossed the river and restored the line, and while they were driving back a larger number with outstanding courage, one of them fell under a multitude of missiles from the higher ground.
passages.notes: The Latin of this work is notoriously rough and the text corrupt in places. 'eum' (twice) is taken as 'cum'. 'corum' is read as 'eorum'. 'nec desinentibus nostris' is obscure. It is rendered as 'since our men did not let up'; it may mean that our men did not stop working.

passages.original: Quae simul est mota, equitatus Caesaris sinistrum cornum premere coepit ita uti eximia virtute proelium facere possent, locus in aciem ad subsidium veniendi non daretur. Ita cum clamor esset intermixtus gemitu gladiorumque crepitus auribus oblatus, imperitorum mentis timore praepediebat. Hic, ut ait Ennius, pes pede premitur, armis feruntur arma, adversariosque vehementissime pugnantes nostri agere coeperunt quibus oppidum fuit subsidio. Ita ipsis Liberalibus fusi fugatique non superfuisset, nisi in eum locum confugisset ex quo erant egressi.
passages.english: As soon as it [the legion] was moved, Caesar's cavalry began to press the left wing, so that although they were able to fight with outstanding courage, no room was given for coming up into the line in support. Thus, when the shouting was mixed with groaning and the clash of swords struck the ears, it hampered the minds of the inexperienced with fear. Here, as Ennius says, foot is pressed by foot, arms are borne against arms, and our men began to drive back the enemy, who were fighting most fiercely and for whom the town served as a refuge. So on the very day of the Liberalia they were routed and put to flight, and [none] would have survived had they not fled back to the place from which they had set out.
passages.notes: The text is corrupt and the syntax uncertain in places. 'cornum' stands for 'cornu'. In the first sentence 'uti … possent' is taken as concessive ('although they were able'). The subject of the singular 'superfuisset' and 'confugisset' is unclear. It may imply 'none [of them]' or 'the enemy force'; some suspect a lacuna. The Liberalia was the festival of Liber on 17 March.
